questions.q: What does a sequence diagram capture that a system context diagram and a data-flow diagram both leave out?
options: The exact ordered timing of messages between participants during one specific transaction
The names of the external systems involved
Which Salesforce objects store data at rest
The overall boundary of the system being documented
questions.explain: Neither a system context diagram nor a DFD specifies order or timing — a sequence diagram exists specifically to show the precise, ordered sequence of messages over time, read top to bottom.

questions.q: On a UML sequence diagram, what does a lifeline represent?
options: A single message passed between two participants
One participant's existence through the duration of the transaction, drawn as a vertical dashed line
The database table a participant writes to
The error-handling path of a transaction
questions.explain: A lifeline is the vertical dashed line dropping from a labeled box, representing one participant (user, system, class, external API) existing through the transaction's timeframe.

questions.q: In the Apex-callout example in this lesson, why does the solid-arrowhead message from the Lightning web component to the Apex controller matter?
options: It shows the call is asynchronous and the component moves on immediately
A solid arrowhead has no specific meaning in sequence diagrams
It shows the call is synchronous — the Lightning web component waits for the Apex method's result before continuing
It indicates the message failed and needs a retry
questions.explain: A solid arrowhead denotes a synchronous call, where the caller waits for a response before continuing — as opposed to an open/stick arrowhead, which denotes an asynchronous, fire-and-forget call.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a sequence diagram showing only the 'happy path' is incomplete?
options: Because UML forbids diagrams without an error path
Because every Salesforce callout automatically retries three times, so the happy path is never accurate
Because Apex does not support synchronous callouts

Because failure handling (timeouts, retries, fallback logic) is exactly the kind of order-dependent detail a sequence diagram is good at making explicit, and it's easy to leave undocumented until an incident forces the question
questions.explain: A sequence diagram's strength is making exact order-dependent behavior explicit — error and retry paths are part of that behavior, and omitting them leaves exactly the detail undocumented that tends to matter most during an incident.

questions.q: Per this lesson, when should an architect reach for a sequence diagram instead of a data-flow diagram?
options: Whenever any data moves between two Salesforce objects, regardless of timing
Only when documenting Apex trigger order of execution, and never for integrations
When the question is behavioral and order-dependent — exact call order, synchronous/asynchronous timing, retries, or error handling during one specific transaction
Sequence diagrams and DFDs are interchangeable and the choice makes no difference
questions.explain: A DFD answers structural questions (what transforms and stores data) without regard to timing; a sequence diagram is for behavioral, order-dependent questions about one specific transaction's exact sequence of calls.
